policy_name: New Hampshire HB 1432 (Deepfakes)
question: What are the exemptions outlined in this legislation for the use of deepfakes, and what conditions must be met to qualify for these exemptions?
answer_1:
1. The exemptions outlined in this legislation for the use of deepfakes are as follows:

   a. An interactive computer service as defined in 47 U.S.C. section 230 for content provided by another party (RSA 243:1, II, IV, a).

   b. Any radio or television broadcasting station or network, newspaper, magazine, cable or satellite radio or television operator, programmer, or producer, Internet website or online platform, or other periodical that publishes, distributes or broadcasts a deepfake as part of a bona fide news report, newscast, news story, news documentary or similar undertaking in which the deepfake is a subject of the report and in which publication, distribution, or broadcast there is contained a clear acknowledgment that there are questions about the authenticity of the materials which are the subject of the report (RSA 243:1, II, IV, b).

   c. Any radio or television broadcasting station or network, newspaper, magazine, cable or satellite television operator, Internet website or online platform, or other periodical when such entity is paid to publish, distribute or broadcast an election communication including a deepfake, provided that the entity does not remove or modify any disclaimer provided by the creator or sponsor of the election communication (RSA 243:1, II, IV, c).

   d. A video, audio, or any other media that constitutes satire or parody or the production of which is substantially dependent on the ability of one or more individuals to physically or verbally impersonate another person without reliance on artificial intelligence (RSA 243:1, II, IV, d; RSA 243:2, II, III, d).

2. To qualify for these exemptions, the content must meet the conditions specified in the legislation. For example, news reports, newscasts, news stories, news documentaries, or similar undertakings must contain a clear acknowledgment that there are questions about the authenticity of the materials which are the subject of the report (RSA 243:1, II, IV, b). Additionally, election communications must not have any disclaimers removed or modified by the entity publishing, distributing, or broadcasting them (RSA 243:1, II, IV
answer_2: 1) Exemptions for deepfakes are outlined in sections II(b), II(c), III(d), 507:8-j(III)(a), 507:8-j(III)(b), and 507:8-j(III)(c) of the legislation. 2) The exemptions apply to bona fide news reports, election communications, satire or parody, and interactive computer services that are merely providing content created by others. 3) For these exemptions to apply, the deepfake must be part of a report, news story, news documentary, or similar undertaking, or the entity must not remove or modify any disclaimer provided by the creator or sponsor of the election communication.

policy_name: New Hampshire HB 1432 (Deepfakes)
question: How does this legislation impact individuals or entities involved in lobbying activities, and what are the consequences for those convicted of offenses related to deepfakes and lobbying?
answer_1:
This legislation impacts individuals or entities involved in lobbying activities by prohibiting the Secretary of State from accepting their registration if they have been convicted of an offense under RSA 638:26-a (Fraudulent Use of Deepfakes) or found liable under RSA 507:8-j (Civil Actions for Fraudulent Use of Deepfakes) related to their lobbying. The consequences for those convicted of offenses related to deepfakes and lobbying are that they will be barred from registering as lobbyists in the state of New Hampshire.

Citation: RSA 15:1 (VI)
answer_2: This legislation impacts individuals or entities involved in lobbying activities by prohibiting the Secretary of State from accepting their registration if they have been convicted of an offense under RSA 638:26-a or found liable under RSA 507:8-j related to their lobbying. Consequences for such individuals or entities include being barred from lobbying activities. (243:3)

policy_name: Countering Communist China Act, Title I ("Trade, Investment, and Economic Relations"), Sec. 102 ("Sanctions for Chinese Military and Surveillance Companies")
question: What specific economic sectors in the People's Republic of China are targeted by the sanctions outlined in Section 102, and what activities within these sectors trigger the imposition of sanctions?
answer_1:
The economic sectors targeted by the sanctions outlined in Section 102 of the Act are the defense and related materiel sector (a) and the surveillance technology sector (a). The activities within these sectors that trigger the imposition of sanctions are those where a foreign person knowingly engages in significant operations in either of these sectors in the economy of the People's Republic of China (a).

Citations:
- Section 102(a) of the Act: "Not later than 180 days after the date of the enactment of this Act, the President shall impose the sanctions described in subsection (e) with respect to any foreign person determined by the Secretary of the Treasury, in consultation with the Secretary of State and, as the Secretary of the Treasury determines appropriate, the Secretary of Defense, to knowingly engage in significant operations in the defense and related materiel sector or the surveillance technology sector of the economy of the People’s Republic of China."
- Section 102(b)(1) of the Act: "Not less frequently than annually, the Secretary of the Treasury shall— (1) undertake the determination described under subsection (a) with respect to foreign persons listed in the Annex to Executive Order 14032 (as amended by any revision to such Annex);"
- Section 102(c)(1)(A) of the Act: "foreign persons listed on the Military End User List (Supplement No. 7 to part 744 of the Export Administration Regulations) that are located in the People’s Republic of China;"
- Section 102(c)(1)(B) of the Act: "foreign persons listed by the Department of Commerce on the Denied Persons List or the Entity List (Supplement No. 4 to part 744 of the Export Administration Regulations) that are located in the People’s Republic of China;"
- Section 102(c)(1)(C) of the Act: "foreign persons listed pursuant to section 1260H of the William M. (Mac) Thornberry National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021 (10 U.S.C. 113 note);"
answer_2: The sanctions outlined in Section 102 target the defense and related materiel sector, as well as the surveillance technology sector of the People's Republic of China. The Secretary of the Treasury, in consultation with other secretaries, is to assess whether foreign persons engaged in significant operations in these sectors should be subject to sanctions. Additionally, the Secretary may focus on foreign persons engaging in activities related to artificial intelligence, high-performance computing, biotechnology, data storage, and other advanced technologies (Section 102(d)).

policy_name: Countering Communist China Act, Title I ("Trade, Investment, and Economic Relations"), Sec. 102 ("Sanctions for Chinese Military and Surveillance Companies")
question: Which U.S. government entities are responsible for determining which foreign persons will be sanctioned under Section 102, and what is the process for making this determination?
answer_1: The determination of which foreign persons will be sanctioned under Section 102 is the responsibility of the Secretary of the Treasury, in consultation with the Secretary of State and, as the Secretary of the Treasury determines appropriate, the Secretary of Defense (SEC. 102(a), (c)). The process for making this determination includes an annual assessment of foreign persons listed on certain lists, focusing on specific activities related to advanced technologies, and submitting reports to the appropriate congressional committees (SEC. 102(b), (c), (d)).
answer_2: The Secretary of the Treasury, in consultation with the Secretary of State and, as the Secretary of the Treasury determines appropriate, the Secretary of Defense, is responsible for determining which foreign persons will be sanctioned under Section 102. The process involves assessing whether sanctions should be imposed with respect to the activities of foreign persons listed on certain lists, focusing on specific technology sectors, and submitting reports to Congress explaining the results of the determination. (cited from document IDs: d1, d4)

policy_name: Countering Communist China Act, Title I ("Trade, Investment, and Economic Relations"), Sec. 102 ("Sanctions for Chinese Military and Surveillance Companies")
question: Summarize the conditions under which the President can waive the sanctions described in Section 102, and what alternative measures are required if a waiver is granted?
answer_1: The President can waive the application of sanctions under Section 102 for renewable periods of one year if the President certifies in writing to the appropriate congressional committees that the waiver is in the national interest of the United States, with an explanation of the reasons therefor (SEC. 102(h)). In lieu of the imposition of such sanctions, the President shall prohibit the purchase or sale of any publicly traded securities, or any publicly traded securities that are derivative of such securities, issued by any person with respect to which sanctions were waived (SEC. 102(h)).
answer_2: The President can waive the sanctions under Section 102 for renewable periods of one year if certified in writing to the appropriate congressional committees that the waiver is in the national interest of the United States, with an explanation of the reasons therefor. In lieu of the imposition of such sanctions, the President shall prohibit the purchase or sale of any publicly traded securities, or any publicly traded securities that are derivative of such securities, issued by any person with respect to which sanctions were waived. policy_name: S. 3004 (Chief AI Officer Governing Council)
question: What are the primary responsibilities and scope of authority granted to the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer (CDAO) under this bill regarding Department of Defense data?
answer_1: The Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer (CDAO) of the Department of Defense, under this bill (S. 3004), is granted the authority, but not the requirement, to access and control all data collected, acquired, accessed, or utilized by Department of Defense components. This authority is subject to section 1513 of the James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023 (Public Law 117–263; 10 U.S.C. 4001 note). The CDAO is also tasked with heading the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer Governing Council, which is established to provide policy oversight for the responsible, coordinated, and ethical employment of data and artificial intelligence capabilities across Department of Defense missions and operations. (Source: S. 3004)
answer_2: The CDAO is granted the authority, but not the requirement, to access and control Department of Defense data under Section 1(a) of S. 3004. This control is consistent with section 1513 of the James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023 (Public Law 117–263; 10 U.S.C. 4001 note). The CDAO is also responsible for heading the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer Governing Council, which provides policy oversight and coordinates the ethical and responsible employment of data and AI capabilities across Department of Defense missions and operations (Section 1(b) of S. 3004).

policy_name: S. 3004 (Chief AI Officer Governing Council)
question: How does the establishment of the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer Governing Council aim to improve the development, implementation, and oversight of AI within the Department of Defense?
answer_1:
The establishment of the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer Governing Council aims to improve the development, implementation, and oversight of AI within the Department of Defense by streamlining the organizational structure related to AI, improving coordination on AI governance with the defense industry sector, establishing and overseeing AI guidance on ethical requirements and protections, identifying, monitoring, and updating recommendations for operational usage of AI, reviewing AI program funding to ensure adherence to established policy, providing periodic status updates on the efforts to develop and implement AI, implementing and overseeing a data and AI educational program, implementing and overseeing a data decree scorecard, and performing such other duties as the Council determines appropriate (S. 3004, Sec. 1(b)(3)(E)).

Citation: S. 3004, Sec. 1(b)(3)(E)
answer_2: The Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer Governing Council aims to improve the development, implementation, and oversight of AI within the Department of Defense by streamlining the organizational structure related to AI, improving coordination with the defense industry sector, establishing and overseeing ethical requirements and protections for AI usage, identifying and monitoring AI operational usage, reviewing AI program funding, providing periodic status updates, implementing a data and AI educational program, and implementing a data decree scorecard (S. 3004, Section 1(b)(3)(E)).

policy_name: S. 3004 (Chief AI Officer Governing Council)
question: What are the key reporting requirements mandated for the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer Governing Council, including the frequency and recipients of these reports?
answer_1: The Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer Governing Council is mandated to submit a report to the Secretary and the congressional defense committees not later than 180 days after the date of the enactment of this paragraph and not less frequently than once every 18 months thereafter. The report should cover the activities of the Council during the period covered by the report. (Source: S. 3004, Section 1(b)(3)(E)(F))
answer_2: The Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer Governing Council is required to submit a report to the Secretary and the congressional defense committees not later than 180 days after the date of enactment and not less frequently than once every 18 months. The report should cover the activities of the Council during the period covered by the report. (S. 3004)

policy_name: S. 3004 (Chief AI Officer Governing Council)
question: Beyond policy oversight, what specific types of AI-related activities and resources (e.g., funding, tools, data) does the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer Governing Council have the authority to review and provide guidance on?
answer_1:
The Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer Governing Council, as established by S. 3004, has the authority to review and provide guidance on several specific types of AI-related activities and resources. These include:

1. Streamlining the organizational structure of the Department as it relates to artificial intelligence development, implementation, and oversight (Section 238(d)(3)(E)(i)).
2. Improving coordination on artificial intelligence governance with the defense industry sector (Section 238(d)(3)(E)(ii)).
3. Establishing and overseeing artificial intelligence guidance on ethical requirements and protections for usage of artificial intelligence supported by Department funding and reducing or mitigating instances of unintended bias in artificial intelligence algorithms (Section 238(d)(3)(E)(iii)).
4. Identifying, monitoring, and periodically updating appropriate recommendations for operational usage of artificial intelligence (Section 238(d)(3)(E)(iv)).
5. Reviewing artificial intelligence program funding to ensure that any Department investment in an artificial intelligence tool, system, or algorithm adheres to all Department established policy related to artificial intelligence (Section 238(d)(3)(E)(v)).
6. Providing periodic status updates on the efforts of the Department to develop and implement artificial intelligence into existing Department programs and processes (Section 238(d)(3)(E)(vi)).
7. Providing guidance on access and distribution restrictions relating to data, models, tool sets, or testing or validation infrastructure (Section 238(d)(3)(E)(vii)).
8. Implementing and overseeing a data and artificial intelligence educational program for the purpose of familiarizing the Department at all levels on the applications of artificial intelligence in their operations (Section 238(d)(3)(E)(viii)).
9. Implementing and overseeing a data decree scorecard (Section 238(d)(3)(E)(ix)).
10. Performing such other duties as the Council determines appropriate (Section 238(d)(3)(E)(x)).

Citation: S. 3004, Section 238(d)(3)(E) (Public Law 115–232; 10 U.S.C. note prec. 4
answer_2: The Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Officer Governing Council has the authority to review and provide guidance on various AI-related activities and resources, including streamlining the organizational structure of the Department as it relates to AI development, improving coordination on AI governance with the defense industry sector, establishing and overseeing AI guidance on ethical requirements and protections, identifying and monitoring AI program funding, providing periodic status updates on the efforts of the Department to develop and implement AI, implementing and overseeing a data and AI educational program, and implementing and overseeing a data decree scorecard (S. 3004, Sec. 1(b)(3)(E)).

policy_name: Framework to Mitigate AI-Enabled Extreme Risks
question: In brief, what are the key components of this framework for overseeing frontier AI models, encompassing hardware, development, and deployment?
answer_1:
The key components of the proposed framework for overseeing frontier AI models include:

1. Hardware: Entities selling or renting large computing resources for AI development must report large acquisitions or usage and exercise due diligence to ensure customers are known and vetted, particularly with respect to foreign persons (citation: Proposal text).

2. Development of Frontier Models: Developers must notify the oversight entity when developing a frontier model and prior to initiating training runs. They are required to incorporate safeguards against the four extreme risks identified and adhere to cybersecurity standards to ensure models are not leaked or stolen (citation: Proposal text).

3. Deployment of Frontier Models: Developers must undergo evaluation and obtain a license from the oversight entity prior to release. A tiered licensing structure would be utilized to determine how widely the frontier model could be shared, with low-risk models being licensed for open-source deployment and higher-risk models being licensed for deployment with vetted customers or limited public use (citation: Proposal text).

4. Oversight Entity: The oversight authorities could be given to a new interagency coordinating body, a preexisting federal agency, or a new agency. Potential options include an interagency coordinating body modeled on CFIUS, the Department of Commerce, the Department of Energy, or a new agency. The oversight entity should be comprised of subject matter experts and skilled AI scientists and engineers, and it should study and report to Congress on unforeseen challenges and new risks to ensure the framework remains appropriate as technology advances (citation: Proposal text).
answer_2: 1) The framework covers the most advanced AI models, known as frontier models, which are those trained on more than 10^26 operations and either broadly-capable or intended for bioengineering, chemical engineering, cybersecurity, or nuclear development. 2) Oversight of hardware involves reporting large acquisitions or usage of computing resources to the oversight entity, and ensuring customers are known and vetted. 3) Developers must notify the oversight entity, incorporate safeguards against extreme risks, and adhere to cybersecurity standards. 4) Frontier model developers must obtain a license from the oversight entity before release, with a tiered licensing structure determining the model's distribution. 5) The oversight entity could be a new interagency body, Department of Commerce, Department of Energy, or a new agency, and should include subject matter experts and AI scientists/engineers. The oversight entity should also study and report on unforeseen challenges and new risks as technology advances.

policy_name: Framework to Mitigate AI-Enabled Extreme Risks
question: What specific types of AI-enabled extreme risks does this framework prioritize mitigating, and how does it propose to achieve this mitigation across the lifecycle of frontier models?
answer_1:
This framework prioritizes mitigating AI-enabled extreme risks in the areas of biological, chemical, cyber, and nuclear threats. The proposed mitigation measures across the lifecycle of frontier models are as follows:

1. Hardware: Entities selling or renting large amounts of computing hardware for AI development are required to report large acquisitions or usage and exercise due diligence to ensure that customers are known and vetted, particularly with respect to foreign persons. (Source: Proposal text)

2. Development of Frontier Models: Developers are required to notify the oversight entity when developing a frontier model and prior to initiating training runs. They must incorporate safeguards against the four extreme risks identified and adhere to cybersecurity standards to ensure models are not leaked prematurely or stolen. (Source: Proposal text)

3. Deployment of Frontier Models: Developers undergo evaluation and obtain a license from the oversight entity prior to release. The evaluation considers whether the frontier model has incorporated sufficient safeguards against the four identified risks. A tiered licensing structure is utilized to determine how widely the frontier model could be shared, with lower-risk models being licensed for open-source deployment and higher-risk models being licensed for deployment with vetted customers or limited public use. (Source: Proposal text)

The oversight entity, which could be a new interagency coordinating body, a preexisting federal agency, or a new agency, would be responsible for studying and reporting to Congress on unforeseen challenges and new risks to ensure that this framework remains appropriate as technology advances. (Source: Proposal text)
answer_2: This framework prioritizes mitigating AI-enabled extreme risks in the areas of biological, chemical, cyber, and nuclear threats. It proposes to achieve this mitigation by requiring oversight of hardware, development, and deployment of frontier models. Hardware oversight involves reporting large acquisitions or usage of computing resources to the oversight entity. Development oversight requires developers to notify the entity, incorporate safeguards against the identified risks, and adhere to cybersecurity standards. Deployment oversight involves evaluation and licensing of frontier models based on risk level. The oversight entity could be a new interagency coordinating body, a preexisting federal agency, or a new agency, and should be comprised of subject matter experts and AI scientists/engineers. The oversight entity would also study and report on unforeseen challenges and new risks to ensure the framework remains appropriate as technology advances. (Document ID: N/A)

policy_name: Framework to Mitigate AI-Enabled Extreme Risks
question: What are the proposed mechanisms for evaluating and licensing frontier models prior to deployment, and how do these mechanisms relate to the level of risk associated with each model?
answer_1:
1. The proposed mechanisms for evaluating and licensing frontier models prior to deployment involve an evaluation process by the oversight entity, followed by the issuance of a license. The evaluation would determine whether the frontier model has incorporated sufficient safeguards against the four identified extreme risks (biological, chemical, cyber, and nuclear threats).

2. The licensing structure would be tiered, with the level of risk associated with each model determining the extent of deployment. For instance, frontier models with low risk could be licensed for open-source deployment, whereas models with higher risks could be licensed for deployment with vetted customers or limited public use.

Citations:

- The specifics of the tiered licensing structure are also outlined in the proposal (Section III: Deployment of Frontier Models).

Source: Proposal for a Framework to Mitigate AI-Enabled Extreme Risks, undated. [Document ID not provided]

This evaluation would only consider whether the frontier model has incorporated sufficient safeguards against the four identified risks. 2) A tiered licensing structure would be utilized to determine how widely the frontier model could be shared. For instance, frontier models with low risk could be licensed for open-source deployment, whereas models with higher risks could be licensed for deployment with vetted customers or limited public use. (Document ID: Not applicable)

policy_name: Framework to Mitigate AI-Enabled Extreme Risks
question: What are the four options presented for the oversight entity, and what are the potential strengths and weaknesses of each option concerning AI governance?
answer_1:
The four options presented for the oversight entity are:

1. Interagency Coordinating Body: This option proposes creating a new, interagency body to facilitate cross-agency regulatory oversight. The potential strength of this option is that it could leverage domain-specific subject matter expertise while ensuring coordination and communication among key federal stakeholders. However, the potential weakness is that it may face challenges in establishing clear decision-making processes and ensuring accountability.

2. Department of Commerce: This option suggests leveraging the National Institute for Standards and Technology (NIST) and the Bureau of Industry and Security within the Department of Commerce to carry out these responsibilities. The potential strength of this option is that NIST has a history of developing standards and best practices for various industries, including AI. However, the potential weakness is that the Department of Commerce may not have the necessary expertise in areas such as biosecurity, chemical security, and nuclear security.

3. Department of Energy (DoE): This option proposes that DoE, with its expertise in high-performance computing and oversight of the U.S. National Laboratories, could handle these responsibilities. Additionally, DoE has experience in handling restricted data, classified information, and national security issues. The potential strength of this option is that DoE has the necessary expertise in areas such as high-performance computing and national security. However, the potential weakness is that DoE's primary focus is on energy, and its resources may be stretched thin if it were to take on additional responsibilities.

4. New Agency: This option suggests that Congress could task a new agency with these responsibilities since frontier models pose novel risks that do not fit neatly within existing agency jurisdictions. The potential strength of this option is that a new agency could be specifically designed to address these novel risks. However, the potential weakness is that creating a new agency could be a lengthy and politically contentious process.

Sources:
- Executive Order 14110: Maintaining American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence (https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2021/03/25/executive-order-on-maintaining-american-leadership-in-artificial-intelligence/)
- Framework to Mitigate AI-Enabled Extreme Risks (https://www.bro
answer_2: 1) Interagency Coordinating Body (CFIUS-like), 2) Department of Commerce (NIST and Bureau of Industry and Security), 3) Department of Energy, and 4) New Agency. The Interagency Coordinating Body (A) could offer cross-agency regulatory oversight, leveraging domain-specific subject matter expertise while ensuring coordination and communication among key federal stakeholders. However, it may face challenges in establishing a clear chain of command and maintaining accountability. The Department of Commerce (B) could utilize its existing resources and expertise in AI development, but it may lack the focus and specialized knowledge required for AI governance. The Department of Energy (C) has expertise in high-performance computing and national security issues, but it may struggle to adapt to the rapidly evolving AI landscape. A new agency (D) could be tailor-made for AI governance, but it would require significant resources and time to establish and could face resistance from existing agencies.

policy_name: Idaho HB 664 (Freedom From AI-Rigged Elections Act)
question: Explain the specific types of synthetic media that the Freedom From AI-Rigged (FAIR) Elections Act targets and provides remedies for.
answer_1: The Freedom From AI-Rigged (FAIR) Elections Act targets synthetic media that is created through the use of generative adversarial network techniques or other digital technology to create a realistic but false audio or video recording of an individual's speech or conduct. This synthetic media is defined as an audio recording or a video recording of an individual's speech or conduct that provides a fundamentally different understanding or impression of the event, action, or speech than a reasonable person would have from the unaltered, original version of the audio recording or video recording (Idaho Code 67-6628A(2)(c)). The Act provides remedies for candidates whose action or speech is deceptively represented through the use of synthetic media in an electioneering communication, including the ability to seek injunctive or other equitable relief prohibiting the publication of such synthetic media, and the ability to bring an action for general damages, special damages, or both against the information content provider (Idaho Code 67-6628A(3), (4)).
answer_2: The Freedom From AI-Rigged (FAIR) Elections Act targets audio and video recordings of an individual's speech or conduct that have been created through the use of generative adversarial network techniques or other digital technology in a manner to create a realistic but false audio or video that provides a fundamentally different understanding or impression of the event, action, or speech than a reasonable person would have from the unaltered, original version of the audio recording or video recording (Section 67-6628A(2)(c) of the Idaho Code). The Act provides remedies for candidates whose action or speech is deceptively represented through the use of synthetic media in an electioneering communication, including injunctive or other equitable relief, general damages, special damages, and attorney's fees (Section 67-6628A(3) and (4) of the Idaho Code).

policy_name: Idaho HB 664 (Freedom From AI-Rigged Elections Act)
question: Summarize the legal recourse available to a candidate whose image or voice is manipulated using synthetic media in electioneering communications, as outlined in the Act.
answer_1: A candidate whose image or voice is manipulated using synthetic media in electioneering communications may seek injunctive or other equitable relief prohibiting the publication of such synthetic media (Section 67-6628A(3)). Additionally, the candidate may bring an action for general damages, special damages, or both against the information content provider. The court may also award a prevailing party reasonable attorney's fees and costs. The provisions of this subsection do not limit or preclude a plaintiff from securing or recovering any other available remedy (Section 67-6628A(4)).
answer_2: A candidate may seek injunctive or other equitable relief, or bring an action for general damages, special damages, or both against the information content provider who manipulates their image or voice using synthetic media in electioneering communications. The court may also award a prevailing party reasonable attorney's fees and costs. An affirmative defense for the information content provider is providing a disclosure stating, "This (video/audio) has been manipulated" in a prominent and easily readable manner for videos, or in a clearly spoken manner for audio-only content. (Section 67-6628A, Idaho Code)

policy_name: Idaho HB 664 (Freedom From AI-Rigged Elections Act)
question: What are the specific conditions under which a medium disseminating electioneering communications can be held liable for synthetic media content under this Act, and what affirmative defenses are available?
answer_1: 1) A medium disseminating electioneering communications can be held liable for synthetic media content under this Act if it removes any disclosure described in subsection (5) of Section 67-6628A, Idaho Code, from the electioneering communication it disseminates (Section 67-6628A(9)(a)). 2) A medium can also be held liable if it changes the content of an electioneering communication such that it qualifies as synthetic media, subject to the affirmative defenses described in this section (Section 67-6628A(9)(b)). 3) Affirmative defenses available for an information content provider include: a) Disclosing that the media has been manipulated in a manner specified in subsection (5) of Section 67-6628A, Idaho Code (Section 67-6628A(5)).
answer_2: 1) A medium can be held liable if it removes any disclosure described in Section 67-6628A(5) of the Act from the electioneering communication it disseminates. 2) A medium can also be held liable if it changes the content of an electioneering communication such that it qualifies as synthetic media, subject to the affirmative defenses described in Section 67-6628A(5) of the Act. 3) Affirmative defenses include displaying the disclosure as required in Section 67-6628A(5)(a) or reading the disclosure as required in Section 67-6628A(5)(b) for video or audio content, respectively.

policy_name: Idaho HB 664 (Freedom From AI-Rigged Elections Act)
question: Describe the required disclosure that must accompany synthetic media used in electioneering communications to avoid legal action under the Freedom From AI-Rigged (FAIR) Elections Act, detailing the specific requirements for both video and audio formats.
answer_1: The required disclosure that must accompany synthetic media used in electioneering communications to avoid legal action under the Freedom From AI-Rigged (FAIR) Elections Act is a statement that reads, "This (video/audio) has been manipulated." For video, the disclosure must be prominently displayed and appear in a size easily readable by the average viewer, and the disclosure must appear for the duration of the video. For audio, the disclosure must be read in a clearly spoken manner and in a pitch that can be easily heard by the average listener at the beginning of the audio, at the end of the audio, and, if the audio is greater than two (2) minutes in length, interspersed within the audio at intervals of no more than two (2) minutes each. (Idaho Code 67-6628A(5))
answer_2: For synthetic media used in electioneering communications, a disclosure stating, "This (video/audio) has been manipulated" must be prominently displayed for the duration of the video in the case of video or read in a clearly spoken manner and in a pitch that can be easily heard by the average listener at the beginning, end, and at intervals of no more than two (2) minutes each in the case of audio. The disclosure must be easily readable or heard by the average viewer or listener. (Section 67-6628A, Idaho Code)

policy_name: FY2021 NDAA, Division A, Title II, Section 227 ("Limitation on contract awards for certain unmanned vessels")
question: What are the key reporting and certification requirements that the Secretary of the Navy must fulfill before awarding a contract for a large unmanned surface vessel (LUSV) or medium unmanned surface vehicle (MUSV)?
answer_1:
1. The Secretary of the Navy must submit a report and certification to the congressional defense committees at least 30 days before awarding a contract for a LUSV or MUSV (SEC. 227(a)).
2. The report must be submitted not later than 60 days after the date of the completion of an independent technical risk assessment for the covered vessel (SEC. 227(c)(1)).
3. The report must include the findings and recommendations of the Senior Technical Authority for the class of naval vessels that includes the covered vessel, and must include such assessment (SEC. 227(c)(1)(C)).
4. The certification must certify that the critical mission, hull, mechanical, and electrical subsystems of the covered vessel have been demonstrated in vessel-representative form, fit, and function, and have achieved performance levels equal to or greater than applicable Department of Defense threshold requirements for such class of vessels or have maturation plans in place to achieve such performance levels prior to transition to a program of record (SEC. 227(c)(2)(A)).
5. The certification must also state that the contract is necessary to meet Department research, development, test, and evaluation objectives for the covered vessel that cannot otherwise be met through further land-based subsystem prototyping or other demonstration approaches (SEC. 227(c)(2)(B)).

Sources:
- Title 10, United States Code, Section 8669b (Senior Technical Authority)
- Section 227 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021 (Reporting and Certification Requirements for Unmanned Vessels)
answer_2: 30 days before awarding a contract for a LUSV or MUSV, the Secretary of the Navy must submit a report and certification to the congressional defense committees. The report should include an independent technical risk assessment, findings and recommendations of the Senior Technical Authority for the class of naval vessels that includes the covered vessel, and the assessment itself. The certification should state that the critical mission, hull, mechanical, and electrical subsystems of the covered vessel have been demonstrated in vessel-representative form, fit, and function, and have achieved performance levels equal to or greater than applicable Department of Defense threshold requirements, or have maturation plans in place to achieve such performance levels prior to transition to a program of record. The contract is necessary to meet Department research, development, test, and evaluation objectives for the covered vessel that cannot otherwise be met through further land-based subsystem prototyping or other demonstration approaches. (Source: SEC. 227 (c))

policy_name: FY2021 NDAA, Division A, Title II, Section 227 ("Limitation on contract awards for certain unmanned vessels")
question: How does this section restrict the integration of offensive weapon systems into covered vessels, and what conditions must be met before such integration can occur?
answer_1:
This section restricts the integration of offensive weapon systems into covered vessels by requiring a certification from the Secretary of Defense that the covered vessel will comply with applicable laws, including the law of armed conflict, and has been determined to be the most appropriate surface vessel to meet applicable offensive military requirements (SEC. 227(d)(1)(A) and (B)). Before such integration can occur, an analysis of alternatives must be completed that describes the capability needs, projected threats, operational environments, operational concepts, operational requirements, status quo and surface vessel alternatives, vessel design, performance, measures of effectiveness, estimated costs, technology readiness assessment, analysis of alternatives, trade-off analysis, sensitivity analysis, conclusions, and recommendations (SEC. 227(e)(2)). The analysis of alternatives must support the determination that the covered vessel is the most appropriate surface vessel to meet applicable offensive military requirements (SEC. 227(d)(2)(B)). The analysis of alternatives must be submitted to the congressional defense committees not later than one year after the date of the enactment of this Act (SEC. 227(e)(1)).

Sources:
- SEC. 227. LIMITATION ON CONTRACT AWARDS FOR CERTAIN UNMANNED VESSELS. Title XVI—National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021, H.R. 6395, 116th Congress, 2nd Session (2020).
- 10 U.S.C. § 8669b. Senior Technical Authority for naval vessels. Title 10, United States Code.
answer_2: This section restricts the integration of offensive weapon systems into covered vessels by requiring a 30-day certification from the Secretary of Defense that the vessel will comply with applicable laws, including the law of armed conflict, and has been determined to be the most appropriate surface vessel to meet applicable offensive military requirements (Sec. 227(d)(1)(A) and (B)). The certification must be made after the completion of an analysis of alternatives that supports such determination (Sec. 227(d)(2)).

policy_name: FY2021 NDAA, Division A, Title II, Section 227 ("Limitation on contract awards for certain unmanned vessels")
question: What elements must be included in the analysis of alternatives (AoA) regarding covered vessels with integrated offensive weapon systems, and what purpose does this AoA serve?
answer_1:
The analysis of alternatives (AoA) regarding covered vessels with integrated offensive weapon systems must include, at a minimum, the following elements:

1. Identification of capability needs applicable to such covered vessels, including offensive strike capability and capacity from the Mark–41 vertical launch system (e(2)(F)).
2. Projected threats (e(2)(B)).
3. Projected operational environments (e(2)(C)).
4. Projected operational concepts (e(2)(D)).
5. Projected operational requirements (e(2)(E)).
6. Status quo (baseline) and surface vessel alternatives able to meet the capability needs identified in subparagraph (A), including modified naval vessel designs, modified commercial vessel designs, new naval vessel designs, and new commercial vessel designs (e(2)(F)(i)-(iv)).
7. Vessel design, performance, and measures of effectiveness of the baseline and each alternative, including a description of critical mission, hull, mechanical, and electrical subsystems (e(2)(G)).
8. Estimated research, development, test, and evaluation cost of baseline and each alternative (e(2)(H)).
9. Estimated lead vessel and average follow-on vessel procurement costs of baseline and each alternative (e(2)(I)).
10. Life-cycle costs of baseline and each alternative (e(2)(J)).
11. Life-cycle cost per baseline vessel and each alternative vessel (e(2)(K)).
12. Life-cycle cost per specified quantity of baseline vessels and alternative vessels (e(2)(L)).
13. Technology readiness assessment of baseline and each alternative (e(2)(M)).
14. Analysis of alternatives, including relative cost and capability performance of baseline and alternative vessels (e(2)(N)).
15. Trade-off analysis (e(2)(O)).
16. Sensitivity analysis (e(2)(P)).
17. Conclusions and recommendations, which if the Secretary of Defense deems it appropriate, shall include the determination required under subsection (d)(1)(B) (e(2)(Q)).

answer_2: The analysis of alternatives (AoA) regarding covered vessels with integrated offensive weapon systems must include, at a minimum, identification of capability needs, projected threats, operational environments, operational concepts, operational requirements, status quo and surface vessel alternatives, vessel design, performance, and measures of effectiveness, estimated costs, technology readiness assessment, analysis of alternatives and trade-off analysis, sensitivity analysis, conclusions, and recommendations (e(2)(A)-(P), (Q)).
